"Lap" has three distinct meanings as a noun, plus important idioms. Here is each one explained fully.

Meaning 1 — The flat surface your thighs form when you sit

This is by far the most common meaning. When you sit down, your upper legs (thighs) become roughly flat and horizontal, creating a natural upward-facing surface. That surface is your lap.

Think of it as a shelf your own body makes when you sit.

  • "The cat curled up in his lap."
  • "She balanced the book on her lap."
  • "He accidentally spilled soup on his lap."

One crucial detail: your lap exists only when you are sitting. The moment you stand up, it disappears. You would never say "the cat is sitting in my lap" while standing — it wouldn't make sense, because there's no lap to sit in.

The lap also carries a strong sense of closeness and comfort. When a small child sits "in someone's lap," the child is sitting on that person's thighs, nestled against their body. It is an intimate, nurturing position, which is why laps are associated with warmth and care.

This is also why a portable computer is called a laptop — it is designed to rest on your lap while you sit. And a lapdog is a dog small enough to sit comfortably on your lap. (The word "lapdog" is also used figuratively for a person who blindly follows and obeys another — "He's the manager's lapdog.")

Meaning 2 — One complete circuit or length (in sports and racing)

In running, cycling, motor racing, and similar sports, a lap is one complete trip around a track — starting from a point and returning to that exact same point, having gone all the way around.

  • "The race is 20 laps long." → The cars circle the track 20 full times.
  • "She completed 8 laps before stopping." → She ran around the oval track 8 times.
  • "He's leading after lap 15." → He is in first place 15 circuits into the race.

In swimming, a lap typically means one length of the pool — swimming from one wall to the other. However, some people (especially in casual use) use "lap" to mean going down and coming back, which would be two lengths. Both usages exist in real life; context usually makes it clear which one is meant.

This meaning is also used loosely and figuratively to describe a stage or stretch of any journey or long task:

  • "We're on the final lap of this project." → We're almost done.
  • "The last lap of the road trip was the most tiring." → The final stretch of the drive.

Meaning 3 — An overlapping section (technical use)

When one flat piece of material is laid on top of another so that one extends over the edge of the other, that overlapping area is called a lap. You will encounter this mainly in construction, carpentry, roofing, and sewing.

  • "The roof shingles have a three-inch lap." → Each shingle overlaps the one below it by three inches, so rain cannot get through the gap.
  • A lap joint in woodworking is a connection where two pieces of wood are joined by each overlapping the other.

This is a specialized, technical meaning. You won't hear it in ordinary conversation, but it is a real and established sense of the word.

A word's full meaning includes the fixed phrases it appears in. These three are important and widely used:

"In the lap of luxury"
Living in great comfort, surrounded by wealth and ease.

  • "They spent the holiday in the lap of luxury."

The image is of being cradled and held by luxury itself, as if sitting in its lap.

"In the lap of the gods"
Something whose outcome is uncertain and completely outside human control — left to fate or chance.

  • "The final score is in the lap of the gods now."
  • "Whether the treatment works is in the lap of the gods."

The idea is that the matter has been handed over to a higher power, and humans can do nothing more about it.

"Fall / drop into someone's lap"
Something comes to a person easily and without effort on their part — they didn't have to seek it out or work for it; it simply arrived.

  • "She wasn't even looking for a job — the offer just fell into her lap."
  • "Opportunities don't usually drop into your lap; you have to go after them."

On your bodyThe flat surface your thighs create when you sit; exists only when seated
In sport/racingOne complete circuit around a track, or one length of a swimming pool
In constructionThe area where one piece of material overlaps another

Those are all the core senses of "lap" as a noun — the body sense, the racing sense, the technical/overlap sense — plus the three most important idioms built around it.
